title: CPU request preemption & work-stealing probes
content:
Purpose
---
Quick exploratory notes on a CPU-side source of tail latency we've been seeing on small payloads: intermittent 5–20ms spikes during tokenization + request preproc. Hypothesis: preemption + work-stealing churn in our Python-backed preproc/parse threadpool is causing scheduling jitter and increased syscalls. This doc captures microbench experiments, sampling, flamegraph snippets, and candidate mitigations to triage further.

Context and symptom
---
- Seen in production: small requests (<= 128 tokens) P95/P99 tokenization stage spikes; overall request P95 higher than model-only latency suggests CPU preproc contribution.
- Reproducible on staging when synthetic load simulating many small concurrent requests (~700 rps across 24 cores).
- Stack traces and perf show lots of context switches, futex/syscall wakeups, and Python interpreter state transitions.

Important constraints
---
- We must keep Python-based preproc for extensibility (custom tokenizers, plugin hooks).
- Can't force exclusive cores for worker threads on all Dedicated customers. Need mitigations that help with scheduling and reduce syscall frequency.

Experiment matrix (summary)
---
Configs tested:
A) baseline: current threadpool (N workers = cpu_count), default Python interpreter, no affinity.
B) limited-parallelism: threadpool size = cpu_count / 2.
C) cooperative-yield shim: insert occasional time.sleep(0) yields in long-running loops to let kernel schedule more fairly.
D) park/unpark prototype: wake-only semantics with a lock-free handoff (pyshim-park-unpark-style).
E) worker-affinity: set pthread affinity to pin workers by CPU groups (4-core groups).
F) GIL-minimizing: move heavy parse paths into short-lived C extension (micro-ffi) to avoid repeated GIL toggles.

Microbenchmark harness
---
- harness spawns N clients sending requests with randomized small payloads (average tok len 40).
- measured metrics: tokenization P50/P95/P99 (ms), request total P50/P95/P99 (ms), context switch rate (syscalls/sec), futex wake count (from perf).
- environment: 24 vCPU, Linux 6.x kernel, python 3.11, jemalloc, no VM balloon.

Results (representative)
---
Baseline (A): tokenization P95 12.8ms, P99 34.5ms, request P95 62ms, ctx-switches 2.2k/s, futex-wakes 940/s
B (half workers): tokenization P95 9.1ms, P99 18.2ms, request P95 48ms, ctx-switches 1.1k/s, futex-wakes 430/s
C (yield): tokenization P95 11.5ms, P99 26.4ms, request P95 55ms, ctx-switches 1.9k/s, futex-wakes 780/s
D (park/unpark): tokenization P95 8.6ms, P99 15.7ms, request P95 46ms, ctx-switches 860/s, futex-wakes 210/s
E (affinity): tokenization P95 9.3ms, P99 17.2ms, request P95 50ms, ctx-switches 1.0k/s, futex-wakes 330/s
F (GIL-min): tokenization P95 7.8ms, P99 13.9ms, request P95 44ms, ctx-switches 520/s, futex-wakes 120/s

Observations
---
1) Reducing number of workers (B) consistently lowers context switch and futex counts and reduces tail latency. This indicates oversubscription + preemption as a major factor.
2) Cooperative yields (C) didn't help much; can actually increase syscall churn because lots of short sleeps trigger scheduler wakeups. Not recommended.
3) Park/unpark design (D) and worker affinity (E) both help, but D reduces futex wakes much more. A lock-free or minimal-wakeup handoff prevents thundering-wakeup behavior.
4) Minimizing GIL hold time by moving parse work into a C path (F) gave the best improvements across tail metrics and materially reduced context switches. Suggests GIL contention + preemption combined to amplify tail latency.

Profiling evidence
---
- perf top / perf record showed high counts in: futex_wait_queue_me requeue, schedule, do_futex, python3.11 PyEval_EvalFrameEx, and native tokenization code.
- Flamegraphs (stack-sampled at 99Hz) show many stacks with: PyThread_acquire_lock -> do_futex -> schedule -> tokenization.parse_loop. The common pattern: Python tries to acquire a lock, gets preempted or blocked, kernel futex wake needed.
- Sampling around a P99 spike captured multiple threads in runnable state but queued on futexes — indicates contention + wakeup storm.

Hypotheses (consolidated)
---
1) Oversubscription: default threadpool size equals core count; when combined with other process-level load (model-server, io threads), kernel preemption causes frequent context switches.
2) Thundering wakeups: our current condition variable / queue implementation wakes many workers on each arrival; if many wake, only one gets the work and the rest repark and cause futex churn.
3) GIL toggles: frequent short Python C API calls that reacquire/release the GIL cause additional scheduler transitions and syscalls.
4) Kernel scheduling latencies amplified by heterogeneous CPU frequency/power states on cloud instances.

Immediate mitigations tested and recommended
---
Short-term (safe):
- Reduce default pool size for small-request endpoints (N = max(2, cpu_count/2)). Simple config flag; immediate P95 wins.
- Configure worker threads with SCHED_OTHER + nice adjustments for preproc threads to reduce priority inversion with model infer threads.

Medium-term (requires code changes):
- Replace condvar-based queue with a wake-minimizing handoff (park/unpark or MPSC enqueue with one-shot notify). Implementation sketch in prototype D shows big wins.
- Introduce optional worker affinity groups (pin sets) for high-density deployments. Provide opt-in config.

Longer-term (larger engineering):
- Move hot parse paths into a small C extension with minimal GIL hold or into a dedicated rust extension (ffi path). Micro-ffi shown in F was best.
- Evaluate user-space scheduler (io_uring + shared submission queues) to reduce kernel wakeups for small tasks.

Open questions and follow-ups
---
- Can we detect overload dynamically and shrink pool size without human config (adaptive pool)? Quick idea: sample queue depth and futex rates and throttle new accept/route policies.
- How does this interact with colocated model inference on same host (Dedicated)? Need to test mixed workloads (GPU CPU helper threads + preproc threads).
- Validate across kernels (5.x vs 6.x) and cloud providers: different wakeup behavior observed in earlier runs.

Bench commands and notes (for replicability)
---
- harness run: python tools/synthetic_load.py --clients 200 --rps 700 --payload small --duration 600 --workers 24
- perf sample: sudo perf record -F99 -a -g -- python -m serving_runtime.stress_harness && sudo perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded && flamegraph.pl out.folded > flame.svg
- futex counters: sudo perf stat -e futex_wait_queue_me_requeue,syscalls:sys_enter_futex -p <pid> sleep 60

Notes / rough TODOs
---
- [ ] Instrument existing threadpool to export futex-wake counters to console (OpenTelemetry) for live dashboards.
- [ ] Merge park/unpark prototype after more safety tests (race windows). PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1189 (draft).
- [ ] Start RFC for small C extension of tokenizer core: include benchmarks, memory safety notes. Owner: Diego.

Appendix: quick code sketches
---
1) One-shot notify queue idea: push work into MPSC queue; if queue was previously empty, call futex_wake(1) to wake only one waiter. Beware ABA and rare lost-wake cases; needs sequence-numbering.
2) Park/unpark pseudo: worker does fast-path try-pop; on miss, register waiter-slot with thread-id and block; producer swaps slot and wakes that specific tid via pthread_kill or futex-based wake. Prototype shows reduced wake counts dramatically.

Summary
---
Our experiments point to a compounded issue: oversubscription + wake-storms + GIL churn. Short-term fixes (smaller pools, thread niceness) are safe and yield clear improvements. Medium-term work (wake-minimizing queue and targeted affinity) offers better sustained tail-latency reductions, but requires careful concurrency correctness work. The most robust gains come from reducing Python GIL involvement for hot paths.

If we prioritize: 1) apply reduced pool defaults + dashboards, 2) land park/unpark after stress testing, 3) plan FFI tokenizer for 2H 2025.

Endnotes
---
- Notes are exploratory and contain rough numbers — re-run harness in your region before using numbers for perf claims.
- Ping me (Jordan) on Slack #eng-serving-runtime for live walkthrough/demos.
